cards.title: 1.1 National income
body: **GDP** = market value of all *final* goods and services produced in one year by factors located *inside* the country (citizens or foreigners).
**GNP** uses ownership (nationals, even abroad) rather than territory. Per capita = GDP (or GNP) ÷ population.

body: Flour sold to a bakery is *intermediate*. Bread sold to a family is *final*. Count the bread (or count value added at each stage) — never flour + bread.

cards.title: Exam-style A — simple GDP table
problem: A toy economy in 2010 produces only two final goods, all bought by households: 500 bicycles sold at 2,000 Nfa each and 500 radios sold at 200 Nfa each.

steps.text: **Given:** two final goods, their prices and quantities.
**Required:** GDP.
GDP = Σ (P × Q) for final goods only.
A longer table with more goods works the same way: multiply each final good’s price by its quantity and add.

cards.problem: C = 80, I = 50, G = 70, X = 80, M = 100 (all million Nfa). Find GDP.

steps.text: Write GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).
Common trap: adding M instead of subtracting.
A trade deficit shrinks measured GDP.

cards.answer: A trade deficit shrinks measured GDP.

cards.title: 1.1.1 Measuring National Economic Performance (National Output)
body: Every society must keep track of its annual output in order to know whether it has produced enough goods and services.
The total flow of final goods and services in a society over a period of time is the national output.
A country’s economic performance is measured over a given period of time by the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Gross National Product (GNP) or National Income (NI).
The performance can be compared with its past years performances.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Methods of Measuring GNP/GDP (National output)
body: As indicated in the simple circular flow of income, the four main categories of expenditures are: • Personal consumption expenditure (C) is the largest component of the aggregate expenditure.
The difference between the value of goods and services exported (X) and the value of goods and services imported to the country (M) is called net export.
Net export (NE = X-M) can be positive, negative or zero.
The income obtained by adding the incomes of the four factors of production is called national income at factor cost.

cards.title: Study steps
body: 1. Read the key definition cards once without notes.
2. Cover the examples and say the rule in your own words.
3. Do the unit exercise; check each why-step before the next question.
4. Replay the match game until you can finish it without peeking.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following represents a leakage (withdrawal) from the circular flow of income and expenditure?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define leakages and injections**
In macroeconomics, a leakage is any income that is diverted away from the main circular flow of domestic consumption. Injections are external additions to the spending flow.

**Step 2: Classify the options**
- Investment ($$I$$), Government Purchases ($$G$$), and Exports ($$X$$) are injections that add spending to the circular flow.
- Savings ($$S$$) is income that households choose not to spend on current consumption, representing a withdrawal of funds from the domestic circular loop.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, **Savings** is the correct leakage.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The market value of all final goods and services produced within the geographic boundaries of a country during a year is defined as:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the boundary constraint of national output measures**
National output is measured either geographically or by resource ownership nationality.

**Step 2: Contrast GDP and GNP**
- Gross National Product (GNP) measures output based on citizen ownership, regardless of location.
- Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures output strictly produced within the physical territory (geographic boundaries) of a country, regardless of who owns the resources.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct definition represents **Gross Domestic Product**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The total value of all final goods and services produced in any country during a particular year is:
cards.why:
**Definition:**
**Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** is the market value of all final goods and services produced **within the borders** of a country in a specific time period (usually a year).
**Result:** D is the correct term.

cards.title: 1.2 Consumption, saving, investment
body: Income Y is either consumed or saved: Y = C + S. Investment I is spending on new capital (machines, buildings, inventories) — not buying old shares.
MPC = ΔC / ΔY MPS = ΔS / ΔY MPC + MPS = 1

cards.title: Tip
body: If income rises by 100 Nfa and consumption rises by 80, MPC = 0.8 and MPS = 0.2. The “extra nakfa” always splits between C and S.

cards.title: Exam-style C
cards.problem: Y rises from 2,000 to 2,500 Nfa. C rises from 1,700 to 2,100 Nfa. Find MPC, MPS and the extra saving.

steps.text: Extra saving = ΔY − ΔC = **100 Nfa**.

cards.title: Formula stickies
body: GDP = Σ P×Q finals GDP = C+I+G+(X−M) MPC+MPS = 1

cards.title: 1.2.1 Consumption
body: Consumption refers to all households’ purchases of consumer goods and services.

The level of aggregate consumption at any given time is basically determined by two factors: • the amount of disposable personal income received by the households, and • the allocation of the disposable personal income across consumption and saving.
The consumption function is the functional relationship between the aggregate consumption expenditure of all households, and their disposable personal income.
The relationship is represented as C = f (Yd), where C is the aggregate consumption expenditure, Yd is the disposable personal income of households, and f is the functional relationship.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Saving
body: Saving is a withdrawal from the income stream as shown in the circular flow of income and expenditure.
Other things being equal, an increase in total savings will make households’ consumption expenditure fall short of their disposable personal income.
APS tends to increase as disposable personal income increases.
MPS shows how many more Nakfa households will save when their disposable incomes increase by one Nakfa.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Investment
body: When a restaurant owner buys tables, chairs,or cooking equipment, he/she is investing.
When a college builds a new library, it is investing.
Business firms invest with the objective to earn more profit by increasing their production.
Investment which adds to capital equipment, in turn leads to the increase in the level of national output and national income.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is strictly excluded when calculating GDP to prevent the error of double counting?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define the double-counting problem**
Double counting occurs if the values of both intermediate inputs and final goods are separately added together, causing national output to be mathematically overstated.

**Step 2: Identify the treatment of intermediate goods**
Intermediate goods (e.g., flour to make bread) are already incorporated into the final retail price of the finished product. Therefore, intermediate transactions are strictly excluded from direct GDP calculations.

**Step 3: Final Result**
**Expenditures on intermediate goods** must be excluded.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is 0.80, the marginal propensity to save (MPS) is:
cards.why:
**Step 1: State the relationship between MPC and MPS**
Since any additional disposable income is either spent or saved, the sum of MPC and MPS must mathematically equal one.
$$MPC + MPS = 1$$

**Step 2: Solve for MPS**
$$MPS = 1 - MPC$$
$$MPS = 1 - 0.80 = 0.20$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
The MPS is **0.20**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If income increases from 500 Nakfa to 600 Nakfa and saving increases from 100 Nakfa to 150 Nakfa, then the Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS) is
cards.why:
**Step 1: Find change in Income ($$ \Delta Y $$).** 
$$ 600 - 500 = 100 $$.
**Step 2: Find change in Saving ($$ \Delta S $$).** 
$$ 150 - 100 = 50 $$.
**Step 3: Calculate MPS.** 
$$ MPS = \Delta S / \Delta Y = 50 / 100 = 0.50 $$.

cards.title: 1.3 Public finance
body: Government spends on goods, services and transfers; it raises **revenue** (tax and non-tax). **Budget:** surplus if revenue > spending, deficit if spending > revenue, balanced if equal.
**Fiscal policy** = using G and taxes to cool or heat the economy (more G or lower tax in a slump).

cards.title: Why G exists
body: Public goods, infrastructure, education, defence, redistribution, to correct markets that fail.

cards.title: Revenue
body: Direct taxes (on income), indirect taxes (on goods), fees, aid, profits of public firms.

cards.title: Exam-style D
cards.problem: Revenue 12 bn Nfa, expenditure 15 bn Nfa. Name the budget and the gap.

steps.text: Compare: 15 > 12 → **deficit**.
Gap = 15 − 12 = **3 billion Nfa**.
How might it be financed?
Borrowing (bonds / loans) — the usual answer.
Printing money is possible but inflationary.

cards.answer: Printing money is possible but inflationary.

cards.title: 1.3.1 The Role of the Public Sector in an Economy
body: In a capitalist market economy, the role of the government is limited to functions such as the maintenance of justice, law and order, and the protection of property rights.
Existence of Public Goods Public goods are different from private goods.
A public good is a good whose consumption cannot be limited to the person who purchased the good only.
The two key properties of a public good are non-rivalry in consumption and non-excludability.

cards.title: 1.3.2 Public Expenditure
body: Public expenditure is the expenditure incurred by the public authorities (central and local governments) to satisfy social wants.
Examples of public expenditure are expenditure on health, education, security, road construction, power supply construction, etc.

The significance of public spending lies in the supply of those essential goods and services by the government for the satisfaction of collective wants which cannot be provided economically and efficiently by the private sector.

Factors Responsible for the Growth of Public Expenditure In modern times, public expenditure in all countries has increased tremendously because of the increased role of the governments in managing their economies.

cards.title: 1.3.3 Fiscal Policy and the Budget
body: A budget is a government financial plan containing details of its policies and programs, estimated receipts and proposed expenditures under different headings, for a specific period, usually one year.
All public sector programs and projects are stated clearly in the budget along with the estimated expenditures.
The Budget is an annual statement of the fiscal policies with corresponding financial plans prepared by the government.
Budgeting can be considered as the nerve centre of a government.

cards.title: 1.3.4 Public (government) Revenue
body: Like any other economic unit, a government needs revenue to finance its activities.
Public revenue includes all government incomes and receipts mobilized from various sources.
The size of public revenue is determined by the strength of an economy and efficiency of the tax collecting authority.
Tax revenue Taxation is the major source of public revenue.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In the consumption function, the 45-degree reference line represents the points where:

options.C: The marginal propensity to consume is zero

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the geometry of the 45-degree line**
On a standard macroeconomic consumption plot, the 45-degree line is the line of perfect equality ($$C = Y_d$$).

**Step 2: Connect to economic meanings**
Every point on this line represents a state where aggregate consumption expenditure exactly equals aggregate disposable income, meaning that household saving is exactly zero ($$S = 0$$).

**Step 3: Final Result**
It represents points where **Consumption expenditure equals disposable income**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The highest expected rate of return or profitability estimated on a new capital asset is called the:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall investment demand determinants**
Firms evaluate investment decisions by comparing the cost of borrowing (interest rate) with the expected profitability of the new capital asset.

**Step 2: Identify the specific economic term**
The expected rate of profit or return on a new capital asset is defined by economists as the **Marginal Efficiency of Capital (MEC)**.

**Step 3: Final Result**
This expected rate of return is called the **Marginal efficiency of capital**.

cards.title: 1.4 International trade
body: No country makes everything. Trade theories: countries gain by specialising where they are better (absolute / comparative advantage).
**Balance of payments:** current account (goods, services, transfers) + capital / financial account. A current deficit can be offset by capital inflow.
**Exchange rate:** price of one currency in another. Demand for nakfa rises if foreigners want Eritrean goods or assets; supply rises if residents want imports.

cards.title: Exam-style E
cards.problem: Exports 40, imports 55, capital inflow 20, capital outflow 8 (million Nfa). Comment on current and overall accounts (simplified).

steps.text: Current ≈ X − M = 40 − 55 = **−15** (deficit).
Capital net = 20 − 8 = **+12**.
Overall ≈ −15 + 12 = **−3** (still a small deficit to finance from reserves or extra borrowing).
If exports had been 45 instead, overall = −10 + 12 = +2 million (a surplus) — same arithmetic, different signs.

cards.answer: Current account −15 million (deficit), capital account +12 million, overall about −3 million Nfa (small deficit).

cards.title: 1.4.1 International Trade Theories
body: Monday through Friday a typical Eritrean worker gets up in the morning and gets ready to go to work.
Before he/she ever leaves the house he/she drinks a cup of tea or coffee, probably with sugar in it.
To get to work, he/she may take a bus or bicycle.
The wheels of the bus or bicycle have rubber tyres on them and the bus engine uses gasoline for fuel.

cards.title: 1.4.2 The International Balance of Payments
body: When countries engage in international trade, they have to record their international transactions in order to know their trade position.
A nation’s balance of payments is a summary statement of a country’s transactions with the rest of the world during a year.

When a country exports goods and services, the value of its exports is recoded as credit (with plus sign) in its balance of payments, while its imports goods and services are recorded as debit (with minus sign) in its balance of payments.
At the end of the year, each nation summarizes its records of total exports and imports of goods and services as well as its other international financial transactions with all other nations.

cards.title: 1.4.3 Exchange Rates
body: The market in which one kind of currency is exchanged for another kind of currency is called foreign exchange market.
The exchange rate, therefore, represents a ratio, i.e. the price of one currency in terms of another currency.
The decrease in the value of domestic currency is called depreciation.
After that, the official exchange rate remains constant regardless of the short terms fluctuations that may be observed in the supply of or demand for foreign currency.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A public good is economically characterized by which of the following properties?

options.C: High transaction costs and high price

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the definition of public goods**
Public goods are distinct from private goods because their physical consumption properties prevent market pricing mechanisms from operating.

**Step 2: State the two properties**
- **Non-rivalry**: One person's consumption does not reduce availability for others.
- **Non-excludability**: Non-payers cannot be excluded from consumption.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, public goods are characterized by **Non-rivalry and non-excludability**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A tax system where the tax rate (percentage of income paid) increases as the taxpayer's income increases is called a:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand tax rate structures**
Taxes are classified into proportional, progressive, or regressive structures based on how the average tax rate changes relative to taxable income.

**Step 2: Evaluate the definitions**
- Proportional: flat rate.
- Regressive: rate falls as income rises.
- Progressive: rate rises as income rises, placing a higher percentage burden on wealthier individuals.

**Step 3: Final Result**
This tax system is a **Progressive tax**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: When the tax decreases with the increase in income, the tax system is;
cards.why:
**Analysis:**
- **Progressive Tax:** Tax rate increases as income increases.
- **Proportional Tax:** Tax rate stays the same for all income levels.
- **Regressive Tax:** Tax rate decreases as income increases (it takes a larger percentage from low-income earners than high-income earners).

cards.title: 2.1.1 Control of Cash
body: The major step in achieving internal control over cash transactions and cash balances include separating the function of handling cash from the maintenance of accounting records.
Cash transactions can be broadly divided into cash receipts and cash disbursements.
The term ‘cash receipts’ refers to cash coming into the business from cash sales, collection of receivables, bank loans, sale of assets, and from other sources.
The term cash disbursement refers to cash payments made by the business for cash purchases, payment of accounts payable, payment of expenses, payment of bank loans, etc.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Petty Cash Fund
body: A petty cash fund is a small cash fund kept in the office for the purposes of making miscellaneous payments.

The operation of a petty cash fund, often called an imprest system (the term “imprest” means an advance of money for a designated purpose), involves three steps: (a) establishing the fund, (b) making payments from the fund, and (c) replenishing the fund.
The fund custodian cashes the cheque and places the proceeds in a locked petty cash box or drawer.
When the custodian of the fund cashes the cheque, the Cash account of business is decreased and the Petty Cash account, another asset account, is increased.

**Step 1: Determine which side of the reconciliation requires entries**
In a bank reconciliation, only the reconciling items on the *book* side (depositor's ledger side) require adjusting journal entries. Bank-side adjustments clear naturally over time.

**Step 2: Evaluate the options**
- Service charges, NSF cheques, and notes collected are unknown to the book until the statement arrives, thus requiring book-side adjustments and journal entries.
- Outstanding cheques are already recorded by the company but not yet by the bank; they adjust the *bank* side and do not require adjusting entries.

**Outstanding cheques** do not require adjusting entries.

cards.title: 2.3.1 Introduction
body: An operating cycle is the length of time between (1) purchase of services or merchandise (products) from suppliers to carry out a business’s activities, and (2) the sale of services or merchandise (products) to customers.
If an item is held for resale to customers, it should be classified as an inventory (current asset) – not plant assets – no matter how durable it is.

For example, a computer that is held for sale by an electronic equipment retailer would be considered inventory, whereas the same computer would be considered a non-current asset for a printing company that buys it for use in operations.
Intangible assets are long term assets which are used in the operation of the business that do not have physical substance and in most cases have to do with legal rights and advantages held.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Accountable events in the lives of plant assets
body: For all categories of plant assets, there are three basic accountable events: (A) acquisition, (B) allocation of the acquisition cost to expense over the asset’s useful life (depreciation), and (C) sale or disposal.
The cost principle requires that companies record plant assets at cost (historical cost).
Cost consists of all expenditures reasonable and necessary for getting the asset to the desired location and ready for its intended use.
For example, the cost of installing and testing a machine is a legitimate cost of the machine.

cards.title: 2.3.3 Controlling plant assets
body: Good internal control requires that each plant asset be separately identified usually with a unique identification number that is either engraved on the asset or attached with a permanent sticker or tag.
Periodically, an inventory of plant assets should be taken to verify the existence, location, condition, and continued use of each asset.
For good internal control, the custodians of the assets must not have access to the records.

In keeping these records, companies usually divide their plant assets into functional groups and provide each group with a separate asset account and accumulated depreciation account in the General Ledger.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Statement presentation of a plant asset and its depreciation
body: Plant assets are shown in the balance sheet at their book values (or carrying values).
Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset account, representing that portion of the asset’s cost that has already been allocated to expenses.
The depreciation methods in use should be disclosed in the notes to the financial statements as per the full disclosure principle.

The correct entry is **Debit Accounts Receivable, Credit Cash**.

questions.q: One of the following is **not** true concerning the Eritrean payroll system?

options.E: Salaried employees earn a fixed amount each pay period.

questions.q: The petty cash fund had an initial imprest balance of $$ $300 $$. The cash left in box equals $$ $60 $$ and petty cash receipts totaling $$ $250 $$ for office supplies. The entry to replenish the fund would contain a

options.A: credit to Cash Over or Short for $$ $10 $$.
options.C: debit to Cash short & over for $$ $10 $$.

why:
**Step 1: Calculate cash needed.** 
Fund Size ($$ 300 $$) - Cash Left ($$ 60 $$) = $$ $240 $$ needed from main bank.
**Step 2: Compare with receipts.** 
Total Receipts = $$ $250 $$. 
**Step 3: Analyze.** 
The accountant has $$ $250 $$ in expense receipts but only needs $$ $240 $$ to bring the box back to $$ $300 $$. This means there is $$ $10 $$ **more cash** than there should be (Overage).
**Step 4: Journal Entry.** 
Dr. Expenses ($$ 250 $$); Cr. Cash ($$ 240 $$); **Cr. Cash Over or Short ($$ 10 $$)**.

questions.q: A company writes a check to replenish a $$ $200 $$ petty cash fund when the fund contains receipts of $$ $194 $$ and $$ $8 $$ in cash. In recording the check, the company should

options.A: Debit Cash Over and Short for $2.

why:
**Step 1: Calculate amount needed to replenish.**
Initial fund = $$ 200 $$. Cash remaining = $$ 8 $$. 
Amount needed = $$ 200 - 8 = 192 $$.
**Step 2: Check for discrepancies.**
Receipts ($$ 194 $$) + Cash ($$ 8 $$) = $$ 202 $$. 
Since we have $$ 202 $$ but should have only $$ 200 $$, we have a $$ $2 $$ **overage**.
**Step 3: Journal Entry.**
Debit Expenses 194; Credit Cash Over and Short 2; **Credit Cash 192**.
